commonLaw.detail: No new common-law marriages may be formed on or after Jan. 1, 2017; valid ones formed earlier still count.

minAge.detail: People 16 or 17 need a notarized consent affidavit from a parent or guardian; anyone under 16 cannot marry.

commonLaw.detail: Alaska stopped recognizing common-law marriages after Dec. 31, 1963; marriages now require a license and solemnization.

minAge.detail: A superior court judge may allow a 16- or 17-year-old to marry after a hearing, finding it is in the minor's best interest, the other party is no more than 3 years older, and parents consent (or withhold consent arbitrarily).

commonLaw.detail: A marriage may not be contracted by agreement without a ceremony; Arizona requires a license and solemnization.

minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds may marry only with custodial parent consent (or emancipation), and the other spouse can be no more than 3 years older; under 16 is barred.

commonLaw.detail: Arkansas courts have long refused to recognize common-law marriages formed in the state, though valid out-of-state ones are honored.
commonLaw.cite: SSA POMS GN 00305.075 (state digest); Furth v. Furth, 97 Ark. 272 (1911)

minAge.detail: A 17-year-old may marry with a notarized affidavit of consent from parents or guardian and a 5-business-day wait; otherwise 18.

commonLaw.detail: Consent alone does not create a marriage in California; it must be followed by a license and solemnization.

minAge.value: No minimum age with court order
minAge.detail: Until Jan. 1, 2027 there is no fixed minimum; anyone under 18 needs a court order. AB 1267 (signed Sept. 30, 2026) sets 18 with no exceptions starting Jan. 1, 2027.

commonLaw.detail: Colorado recognizes common-law marriages, but one formed on or after Sept. 1, 2006 is valid only if both partners were 18 or older.

minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds need a juvenile court order (with a guardian ad litem best-interests review); under 16 cannot marry.

commonLaw.detail: Connecticut does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state; a marriage requires a license and solemnization.

minAge.detail: Both parties must be at least 18; the former exception for 16- and 17-year-olds was repealed in 2023 (P.A. 23-44).

commonLaw.detail: Delaware does not allow common-law marriages to be formed in the state, though it honors valid out-of-state ones.

minAge.detail: No one under 18 may be granted a marriage license in Delaware.

commonLaw.detail: D.C. recognizes common-law marriage based on an express, mutual present-tense agreement to be married followed by cohabitation.
commonLaw.cite: SSA POMS GN 00305.075 (state digest); East v. East, 536 A.2d 1103 (D.C. 1988)

minAge.detail: The age of consent to marry is 18, and the Clerk may not issue a license to anyone under 18.

commonLaw.detail: Common-law marriages entered into after Jan. 1, 1968 are void in Florida; earlier ones remain valid.

minAge.detail: A 17-year-old may marry with written parental consent if the other party is no more than 2 years older; otherwise 18.

commonLaw.detail: No common-law marriage may be entered into in Georgia on or after Jan. 1, 1997; earlier ones remain valid.

minAge.detail: A 17-year-old may marry only if legally emancipated (at least 15 days earlier), the other party is no more than 4 years older, and premarital education is completed; under 17 cannot marry.

commonLaw.detail: A valid Hawaii marriage requires a license and a ceremony performed by an authorized person, so common-law marriages cannot be formed in the state.

minAge.detail: The general minimum is 16 with parental consent; a 15-year-old may marry with written family court approval plus parental consent.

commonLaw.detail: Idaho requires a license and solemnization; common-law marriages formed before Jan. 1, 1996 remain valid.

minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds need written parental consent and cannot marry an adult 3 or more years older; under 16 cannot marry.

commonLaw.detail: Common-law marriages contracted in Illinois after June 30, 1905 are invalid.

minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds may marry with the consent of both parents or a guardian, or with judicial approval.

commonLaw.detail: A common-law marriage entered into in Indiana after Jan. 1, 1958 is void.

minAge.detail: A 16- or 17-year-old needs a juvenile court order approving the marriage and emancipating them, and the age gap can't exceed 4 years.

commonLaw.detail: Iowa recognizes common-law marriages formed in the state.

minAge.value: 16 with parental consent and court approval
minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds need written parental consent plus approval from a district court judge.

commonLaw.detail: Kansas recognizes common-law marriage, but not if either party is under 18.

minAge.detail: A judge may authorize marriage at 15 if in the minor's best interest; 16- and 17-year-olds need parental consent (or a judge's consent).

commonLaw.detail: Kentucky voids any marriage not solemnized or contracted in the presence of an authorized person or society.

minAge.detail: Marriage under 18 is void except that a 17-year-old with parental consent may petition family or district court for permission to marry.

commonLaw.detail: Louisiana requires a marriage ceremony; common-law marriages cannot be formed in the state.

minAge.value: 16 with parental consent and court approval
minAge.detail: A 16- or 17-year-old needs judicial authorization plus written consent of both parents (or tutor/custodian); no marriage under 16.

commonLaw.detail: Maine does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state.

minAge.detail: A marriage license may not be issued to anyone under 18; the exception for 17-year-olds was repealed in 2025.

commonLaw.detail: Maryland does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state, though it honors valid out-of-state ones.

minAge.detail: A 17-year-old may marry with consent of each living parent or guardian (or certain medical/court documentation); under 17 cannot marry.

commonLaw.detail: Massachusetts does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state.

minAge.detail: No magistrate or minister may solemnize a marriage if either party is under 18.

commonLaw.detail: Consent alone is not enough to create a marriage on and after Jan. 1, 1957; a license and solemnization are required.

minAge.detail: A marriage may not be contracted by anyone under 18, and such a marriage is void.

commonLaw.detail: Marriages after April 26, 1941 without a license and solemnization are void.

minAge.detail: Only a person who has reached 18 can marry; Minnesota ended underage exceptions in 2020.

commonLaw.detail: Marriages after April 5, 1956 require a license and ceremony or are void; earlier common-law marriages remain valid.

minAge.detail: Statutory minimums are 17 for males and 15 for females (with parental consent under 21), but a judge may waive the age minimum with parental consent.

commonLaw.detail: Missouri law declares common-law marriages null and void.

minAge.detail: No recorder may issue a marriage license to anyone under 18.

commonLaw.detail: Montana's marriage statutes expressly do not invalidate common-law marriages.

minAge.value: 16 with parental consent and court approval
minAge.detail: A district court may approve marriage for a 16- or 17-year-old who has parental consent, after required marriage counseling.

commonLaw.detail: Nebraska requires a license and solemnization; common-law marriages formed in the state after 1923 are invalid.
commonLaw.cite: Neb. Rev. Stat. § 42-104; Ropken v. Ropken, 169 Neb. 352 (1959)

minAge.detail: Both parties must be at least 17; because the age of majority is 19, minors need written parental consent.

commonLaw.detail: Nevada requires solemnization; only consent-based marriages in effect before March 29, 1943 remain valid.

minAge.value: 17 with parental consent and court approval
minAge.detail: A 17-year-old needs a parent's or guardian's consent plus district court authorization; under 17 cannot marry.

commonLaw.detail: New Hampshire recognizes a common-law marriage only after one partner dies, if the couple lived together and held themselves out as married for at least 3 years.

minAge.detail: No one under 18 can contract a valid marriage (effective Jan. 1, 2025).

commonLaw.detail: Since Dec. 1, 1939 a marriage without a license and authorized ceremony is void.

minAge.detail: No marriage or civil union license may be issued to anyone under 18.

commonLaw.detail: New Mexico does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state.

minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds need consent of each living parent or a district court order; under 16 requires children's court authorization (only in pregnancy or paternity-support cases).

commonLaw.detail: New York has not recognized new common-law marriages since Apr. 29, 1933, but honors ones validly formed in other states.

minAge.detail: Any marriage in which either party is under 18 is prohibited.

commonLaw.detail: A valid North Carolina marriage requires consent expressed before an authorized officiant (or approved religious ceremony), so common-law marriages can't be formed in-state.

minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds need parental consent or a court order and can marry someone no more than 4 years older; under 16 is unlawful.

commonLaw.detail: North Dakota does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state, but recognizes valid out-of-state ones.

minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds need the consent of their parents or guardian; no license may issue to anyone under 16.

commonLaw.detail: Common-law marriages are prohibited on and after Oct. 10, 1991; earlier ones (and valid out-of-state ones) remain valid.

minAge.detail: The general age is 18; a 17-year-old may marry only after a juvenile court consents.

commonLaw.detail: Oklahoma recognizes common-law marriage where the couple mutually agree to be married, have a permanent, exclusive relationship with cohabitation, and hold themselves out as married.

minAge.detail: Until Nov. 1, 2026, 16- and 17-year-olds may marry with parental consent (under 16 only by court order in limited cases). SB 504 (2026) sets 18 with no exceptions from Nov. 1, 2026.

commonLaw.detail: Oregon does not allow common-law marriages to be formed in the state, but recognizes ones valid where formed.

minAge.detail: Marriage requires both parties to be at least 18; the parental-consent exception for 17-year-olds was repealed in 2025.

commonLaw.detail: No common-law marriage contracted after Jan. 1, 2005 is valid; earlier ones remain valid.

minAge.detail: No marriage license may issue if either applicant is under 18 (since 2020).

commonLaw.detail: Rhode Island recognizes common-law marriage, which must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.

minAge.detail: A marriage license may be granted only to a person who is at least 18 (since June 7, 2021).

commonLaw.detail: The S.C. Supreme Court abolished new common-law marriages as of July 24, 2019; ones formed earlier remain valid.
commonLaw.cite: SSA POMS GN 00305.075 (state digest); Stone v. Thompson, 428 S.C. 79 (2019)

minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds need a sworn consent affidavit from a parent, relative, or guardian; under 16 cannot get a license.

commonLaw.detail: Marriages must be solemnized and recorded; common-law marriages consummated before July 1, 1959 remain valid.

minAge.value: 16 with parental consent or court approval
minAge.detail: The general age is 18 (2026 law); 16- and 17-year-olds may marry with a circuit court order or notarized parental consent, and the age gap can't exceed 4 years.

commonLaw.detail: Tennessee does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state (though a long-cohabiting couple may be estopped from denying a marriage in limited cases).

minAge.detail: A 17-year-old may marry with sworn parental or guardian consent if the other party is less than 4 years older; no license for anyone under 17.

commonLaw.detail: Texas recognizes informal (common-law) marriage when a couple agrees to be married, lives together in Texas, and represents themselves as married, or signs a declaration.

minAge.detail: No license may issue to anyone under 18 unless a court has removed the disabilities of minority (emancipation).

commonLaw.detail: A court can validate an unsolemnized marriage if the couple cohabited and held themselves out as married, but a 2026 law bars new petitions on or after May 5, 2027.

minAge.value: 16 with parental consent and court approval
minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds need parental or guardian consent plus juvenile court authorization; otherwise marriage under 18 is void.

commonLaw.detail: Vermont does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state.

minAge.detail: A town clerk may not issue a marriage license if either party is under 18.

commonLaw.detail: Virginia does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state.

minAge.detail: The minimum age at which persons may marry is 18.

commonLaw.detail: Washington does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state, but recognizes valid out-of-state ones.

minAge.detail: Both parties must be 18; any marriage in which a party is under 18 is void.

commonLaw.detail: West Virginia does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state.

minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds may marry with written parental or guardian consent if the other party is no more than 4 years older.

commonLaw.detail: Wisconsin has not recognized common-law marriages formed in the state since 1917, but honors valid out-of-state ones.
Wyoming does not recognize common-law marriages formed in the state, but recognizes ones valid where formed.

minAge.value: 16 with parental consent and court approval
minAge.detail: 16- and 17-year-olds need parental consent and approval from a Wyoming judge (unless emancipated); under 16 marriages are void.
